headline: Common Cholesterol Drug May Slow Vision Loss From Glaucoma
meta_description: New research shows people with glaucoma taking statins need surgery less often and face lower risk of blindness from this leading cause of irreversible vision…
summary_short: A major study of 210,000 statin users finds the cholesterol drug linked to significantly lower rates of glaucoma surgery and vision decline.
body:
Researchers at the University of California in San Diego have discovered that statins—medications millions take daily to manage cholesterol—may offer an unexpected benefit: protecting people from glaucoma, the progressive eye disease known as the "silent thief of sight." A new study published in the British Journal of Ophthalmology analyzed data from 165 million people and found that patients already diagnosed with glaucoma who take statins are substantially less likely to need surgery or other intensive treatments to control the condition. After five years, statin use was associated with a 36% lower risk of requiring traditional glaucoma surgery and a 55% reduced risk of minimally invasive keyhole procedures. Even laser treatments showed promise—statin users had a 60% lower risk of needing selective laser trabeculoplasty, a procedure that lowers pressure inside the eye.

The mechanism remains partly mysterious. "Statins are prescribed to lower cholesterol levels, but studies have indicated that they may also prevent or slow nerve cell death," explained study author Dr. Robert Weinreb. Glaucoma damages the optic nerve gradually, often without noticeable symptoms until significant vision loss occurs, making it a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide.

The research compared over 210,000 people with documented statin use between 2006 and 2026 against a matched control group of 210,000 non-users, all with recorded eye follow-ups. Beyond surgery prevention, statin use was linked to a 12% reduced risk of needing prescription eye drops—the most common first-line treatment for glaucoma. These protective effects persisted even after 10 years of follow-up. While the study is observational and cannot prove statins directly cause these improvements, the findings add meaningful weight to growing evidence that these widely-used drugs may offer neuroprotective benefits beyond their primary purpose.
quick_facts: Study tracked 210,000 statin users vs. 210,000 non-users across 165 million people
Statin use linked to 36% lower risk of glaucoma surgery within five years
University of California, San Diego led the research
Results published in British Journal of Ophthalmology
